title: Apollo 11 · From Earth to the Moon
description: A caption-led journey with Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins, from Saturn V launch to Pacific splashdown.
accuracy: Historical event times and JPL Earth–Moon context. Spacecraft paths, attitudes, staging and terrain are illustrative reconstructions, not recovered flight telemetry. Weather and texture registration are approximate.

captions.text: 16 July 1969. Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins leave Pad 39A aboard a three-stage Saturn V.
Five F-1 engines lift the complete stack. The rocket gradually pitches eastward: reaching orbit requires sideways speed, not just height.
The first stage has spent its propellant. Its tanks and five engines are no longer useful weight.
At about T+2:44, the S-IC separates. The S-II second stage takes over with five J-2 engines.
The interstage and launch escape tower are discarded as the crew climbs beyond the dense atmosphere.
The second stage has accelerated Apollo toward orbital speed. Now the lighter third stage must finish the job.
At about T+9:15, the S-II separates. The single J-2 engine of the S-IVB ignites.
Apollo reaches a low Earth parking orbit. The crew and controllers check the spacecraft before committing to the Moon.
The S-IVB stays attached. Its engine will restart to push Apollo out of Earth orbit.
After the checks, the S-IVB restarts. This burn raises Apollo's speed enough to send it toward the moving Moon.
Apollo is now on a transfer trajectory. The Moon will travel a considerable distance before the spacecraft arrives.
Columbia, the command and service module, separates from the third stage. Eagle is still carried inside the adapter.
Collins turns Columbia through 180 degrees and carefully approaches Eagle nose first.
The docking connection is made. Columbia can now pull Eagle free. The two spacecraft will travel together to the Moon.
Nearly three days of travel are condensed into this chapter. The docked spacecraft coasts while the crew navigates and checks its systems.
The curved route is an educational reconstruction. It shows the changing Earth–Moon geometry, rather than a straight-line flight toward a stationary destination.
Apollo passes behind the Moon. Without braking, it would fly past rather than remain in orbit.
The service propulsion engine fires opposite the direction of travel. Columbia and Eagle enter lunar orbit together.
Armstrong and Aldrin transfer to Eagle. Collins remains alone aboard Columbia in lunar orbit.
Eagle undocks at about 100 hours 12 minutes. Its descent engine will lower its orbit and then brake for landing.
Eagle begins powered descent. The descent engine must remove orbital speed while controlling the fall toward the surface.
Near the surface, Armstrong steers past an unsuitable area. This view illustrates the manoeuvre; the terrain is not a reconstruction of his exact view.
Contact. Eagle settles onto the Moon. The descent stage becomes a landing platform and, later, a launch pad.

media.credit: NASA - Eagle has landed, crew and Mission Control

captions.text: 20 July 1969. Two people have reached the Moon while a third keeps their return spacecraft in orbit.
Armstrong and Aldrin later explore outside, collect samples and deploy experiments. This first edition shows the landed spacecraft; astronaut animation will come later.
The crew spends roughly 21½ hours on the surface. The next chapter skips ahead to lunar liftoff.
Eagle's ascent engine ignites. Only the upper cabin and ascent stage return to lunar orbit.
The gold-clad descent stage and landing legs remain at Tranquility Base. Leaving that mass behind saves ascent propellant.
Reaching orbit is only the beginning: Eagle must rendezvous with Columbia at the right place and time.
A series of orbital manoeuvres brings the ascent stage back to Columbia. The close approach is shown at a watchable pace.
Docking takes place at about 128 hours 3 minutes. Armstrong, Aldrin and the lunar samples return to Columbia.
After the crew transfers, Eagle's ascent stage is discarded. Columbia's service engine must now send all three astronauts home.
The trans-Earth injection burn begins behind the Moon. Only the command and service modules make the return journey.
The return coast spans more than two days. The spacecraft approaches Earth while the Moon continues along its orbit.
The command module's heat shield will absorb the re-entry heating. The service module is no longer needed once entry preparations are complete.
The service module separates. Only Columbia's command module returns through the atmosphere, heat shield first.
Atmospheric drag slows the capsule. The heating effect here is illustrative; this is not an aerothermal simulation.
Three main parachutes slow the final descent toward the Pacific Ocean.
24 July 1969. Splashdown after 195 hours, 18 minutes and 35 seconds. All three astronauts are home. Stop mission returns you to your observatory.
